alt: A two-by-two grid. Rows ask what a plastic is made from: fossil fuels or biological materials. Columns ask what happens at end of life: biodegradable or non-biodegradable. Conventional plastics are made from fossil fuels and are generally non-biodegradable. Bioplastics, made from biological materials, fill both columns: they can be biodegradable or non-biodegradable.
caption: Raw material and end of life are separate questions: a bioplastic can be non-biodegradable.

alt: A biodegradable plastic is decomposed by bacteria and fungi in water or soil into water, biomass, carbon dioxide and, where oxygen is scarce, methane. The rate depends on biotic factors (the decomposers present) and abiotic factors (temperature, moisture, oxygen, light, thickness): fast in industrial composting, slow in cold, dark, deep sea water.
caption: Decomposers turn biodegradable plastic into water, biomass, CO2 and methane, at a rate set by conditions.

alt: Route 1: sunlight, waves and abrasion break non-biodegradable plastic, such as a bottle, into ever smaller fragments. Route 2: tiny particles are made for commercial products such as cosmetics, scrubs and cleaning products, and fibres are shed when synthetic clothes are washed. Microplastics are less than 5 mm long, small enough to pass through filters and be eaten by plankton.
caption: Microplastics come from breakdown of larger plastic and from products made with them.

alt: Four panels. Visual pollution: litter on a beach spoils coasts and tourism. Entanglement: nets, ropes and loops trap turtles, seals, seabirds, fish and whales. Mistaken for food: a floating bag looks like a jellyfish to a turtle. Bioaccumulation and biomagnification: plastic and its chemicals build up from plankton to fish to predators and people.
caption: Plastic harms marine life by looks, by trapping, by being eaten and by building up in food chains.

alt: Plastic moves from use, to waste, to rivers and the sea. Alternative packaging and avoiding single-use plastics reduce the total used; safe disposal and recycling stop waste leaking to rivers and the sea; legislation and enforcement, such as bans on microbeads, dumping and littering, back them all up.
caption: Cut the amount used, stop waste leaking out, and back both with laws.

alt: A bar chart of mass lost in 12 weeks. Plastic A lost 60% in moist soil and 10% in cold seawater; plastic B lost nothing in either. A behaves as a biodegradable plastic, decomposing six times faster in soil; B behaves as non-biodegradable. Repeats and temperature records would improve the test.
caption: Plastic A lost 60% in soil but 10% in cold seawater; B lost nothing.

after: ## Worked example 2: an annotated model answer
alt: Four steps, each worth a mark. Plankton and small fish mistake microplastics for food; toxic chemicals on the plastic build up in each fish (bioaccumulation); the seabird eats many fish so its concentration is much higher (biomagnification); the bird’s health and breeding success suffer. Dots show rising concentration.
caption: Four marks: eaten, accumulates, magnifies, harms the bird.
